what: Marriott franchises and manages hotels rather than owning them. It licenses about thirty brands, from Ritz-Carlton to Courtyard, to hotel owners who pay it fees, and it runs the Bonvoy loyalty programme that fills those rooms.
customers: Hotel owners and developers who pay franchise and management fees; travellers who book through its brands and loyalty programme.
money: a share of room revenue from hotels owned by others
running hotels for owners for a fee
loyalty programme, credit-card partnerships and residential branding
moat: The largest hotel loyalty programme, which gives owners a reason to carry its brands, and a global pipeline of roughly 4,100 hotels under development.
risks: Travel demand falls sharply in recessions and crises
It earns a share of room revenue, so weak pricing hits it directly
Chinese travel demand has been slow to recover
Owners can switch brands when contracts expire
opportunities: Owning almost no hotels means high returns on capital and little capital spending
Credit-card and loyalty fees are stable revenue that does not depend on room rates
The development pipeline adds rooms and fees without company investment
watch: Revenue per available room across regions and net rooms growth.
